name: The London Plane of De Kring
age_estimate: roughly 120 years, from a registered planting decade
access: Free. Public square (plein) owned by the municipality, register: visitable ja, visible ja, openbaar ja. No hours; open at all times.
transport: Roosendaal station is about 0.8 km north, roughly a 10 minute walk via Stationsstraat and Kerkstraat.
story:
The national tree register describes this London plane by the tree behind it. About 13 metres west stands the Oriental plane of De Kring, one of the two species the London plane was bred from, so this corner of the square puts a hybrid and its parent side by side.

This is the front tree and the younger of the pair, banded by the register to a planting between 1900 and 1910, which makes it roughly 116 to 126 years old. The register gives it 25 metres of height to the Oriental plane's 22, and a trunk 3.6 metres round at chest height.

The pair have not had an easy century. In 2002 the Bomenstichting, the Dutch tree foundation, studied the ground beneath them and advised keeping both planes. Building went ahead anyway, inside the spread of their crowns and their roots. When the register last checked, in July 2023, it was mostly the Oriental plane behind whose crown had gone thin, with dead tips on its branches. This one is not the tree it describes as declining.

A horse chestnut once made this a trio. The register records it felled in 2014 and a young tree planted in its place, so that young tree is not part of the old group.

The register is the only source for this tree, and July 2023 is the last time it was recorded standing. If you have walked past it since, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the front one of the two old planes in this corner of De Kring, in its own round tree pit. The rarer Oriental plane stands about 13 metres west, behind it.
verify_notes: Source: LRMB register only (one official register; flagged 'register only', but the record carries a dated inspection: Laatste_waarneming 2023-07-28, status Monumentaal, so vitality was last seen in 2023). Register: Gewone plataan, planting band 1900-1910 (age band, ~116 to 126 years now), girth 360 cm, height 25 m (register figures, undated), solitary, owner gemeente, setting plein. The register note on this record: the oriental plane no. 1680199 stands behind this tree. In 2002 the Bomenstichting did a growing-site study and advised keeping the planes; building was nevertheless done inside the crown projection and rooting zone, and by July 2023 the register notes the crown of mostly the oriental plane had gone thin with dead branch tips. This plane (the front tree) is not the one described as visibly declining. PIN: register point 51.533430, 4.458809 lands on the round tree pit with one clear crown in the PDOK orthophoto (leafless frame, tree stands in a ring pit); the Oriental plane (roo_001, no. 1680199) is a separate crown about 13 m west, not folded because it is a different species and trunk, but both stand in the same corner of the square so the writer should treat them as a pair at one place to stand. The register also records a white horse chestnut (no. 1680201) here felled in 2014 and replaced by a young tree; do not confuse. lifecheck.py returned NONE (no photo evidence); alive rests on the register's 2023 observation. Search for 1987 photograph: register cites westbrabantsarchief.nl photo showing the back tree (the oriental plane) in 1987, not this tree.

name: The Baumann's Horse Chestnut of the Algemene Begraafplaats
age_estimate: roughly 150 years, from a registered planting decade

location.address: Roosendaal, Bachlaan 1, Algemene Begraafplaats (closed municipal cemetery)

verified_sources: https://lokaleregelgeving.overheid.nl/CVDR10613 (Verordening op het beheer en het gebruik van de gesloten gemeentelijke begraafplaatsen, art. 2 para 1: open to everyone daily 8.00 to 16.30)
access: Free. Municipal closed cemetery, open to everyone daily 8.00 to 16.30 (municipal cemetery regulation, art. 2; Oorlogsgraf.nl gives the same hours and says dogs are not allowed). Register: visitable ja, owner gemeente.
transport: About 1.5 km east of Roosendaal station, roughly a 20 minute walk via Bredaseweg; parking for about 10 cars in front of the cemetery.
story:
Every May this horse chestnut covers itself in white flowers, and every autumn it drops not a single conker. It is 'Baumannii', the double-flowered clone of the ordinary horse chestnut, and its flowers set no fruit.

The national tree register bands its planting to the 1870s, roughly 146 to 156 years ago. Sources disagree on when the Algemene Begraafplaats itself opened, somewhere between about 1880 and 1894, so the tree may be as old as the cemetery or older. Nobody has recorded how it came to stand here.

It has seen the cemetery's whole working life. Roosendaal buried its dead here until 1978, when the ground closed to new burials, and the chestnut stayed on among the grave rows, alone, 18 metres tall and 3.64 metres round at chest height.

Age has left its mark. The register notes a split in the main fork with small cracks beneath it, and in December 1999 the crown was thinned and anchored. It was inspected again in May 2025 and is still listed as monumental.

That register is the only record of this tree we have found; if you know its history, tell us. The cemetery is open daily from 8.00 to 16.30, and dogs are not allowed.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the lone big horse chestnut among the grave rows, 3.64 metres round, with no other crown within about 8 metres. In May its flowers are double, and in autumn it bears no conkers.

best_time.label: May, when double white flower candles cover the crown

verify_notes: Source: LRMB register (official) plus the municipal regulation for the access hours; flagged 'register only' for the tree itself, but the record has a dated inspection (Laatste_waarneming 2025-05-22, status Monumentaal), so it was seen alive in 2025. Register: Witte paardenkastanje 'Baumannii' (the double-flowered, fruitless clone of the white horse chestnut), planting band 1870-1880 (age band, ~146 to 156 years now), girth 364 cm, height 18 m, solitary, setting begraafplaats, owner gemeente. Register remark: split in the fork ('plakoksel') with small cracks beneath; crown thinned and anchored in December 1999. PIN: register point lands on one isolated bare crown standing among the grave rows in the PDOK orthophoto, with no neighbouring crown within ~8 m, so the individual tree is placeable. Cemetery founding date varies by source (about 1880 to 1894) and it closed to burials in 1978; the tree's planting band predates or matches the cemetery's start, no bridge claim made. Two other register trees by the cemetery entrance (silver maple no. 1690555, 325 cm; London plane no. 1690554, 287 cm, both about 50 m north) stand in dense woodland in the orthophoto and could not be placed individually: filed as leads. lifecheck.py returned NONE.

name: The Copper Beech of Nispen Cemetery
age_estimate: roughly 175 years, from a registered planting decade

location.address: Nispen, Heijbeeksestraat, at the entrance of the parish cemetery

access: Free. Stands at the cemetery entrance beside the public Heijbeeksestraat and is visible from the street. Register: visitable ja, visible ja, openbaar ja, owner a religious body (parish). No cemetery hours found.
transport: Nispen is about 6 km south of Roosendaal station (about 20 minutes by bike or car); a bus connection was not confirmed, check 9292 for the Nispen stop. 650 m from the Julianalinde (roo_013).
story:
The thickest beech in Roosendaal's part of the national tree register is really three trunks grown into one. At chest height the copper beech at the gate of Nispen's parish cemetery measures 4.9 metres round, more than any other beech the register lists for Roosendaal. Look lower and the trick shows: 40 centimetres above the ground it is three stems, fused higher up into one flat, oval column. The register says so itself, so read the 490 as the girth of a fused mass rather than of a single trunk.

The height needs no footnote. It stands 26 metres tall, a purple crown over the corner where the cemetery entrance meets Heijbeeksestraat.

The Bomenstichting's Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen puts its planting in the decade 1840 to 1850, which makes it roughly 175 years old. That register is the only source behind this entry, but it is a recent one: an inspector looked at the tree in September 2023 and kept it on the list as monumental. The ground belongs to the parish of the Maria Hemelvaartkerk, whose church stands in front of the cemetery.

You can see it from the street without going in. Nispen lies about six kilometres south of Roosendaal, close to the Belgian border, and the lime the village planted in 1909 for the birth of Princess Juliana stands 650 metres away.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its purple-leaved crown, 26 metres tall, on a trunk that splits into three stems just above the ground. It stands at the cemetery entrance on the corner with Heijbeeksestraat, behind the Maria Hemelvaartkerk.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the purple leaves turn copper before they fall

name: The Julianalinde of Nispen

location.address: Nispen, corner of Dorpsstraat and De Lind

verified_sources: https://www.heemkundenispen.nl/oranjebomen_julianalinde.htm (Heemkundekring de Heerlijckheijd Nispen: Julianalinde, planting 24 May 1909, adopted 1993)
access: Free. Municipal green triangle (plantsoen) at a village street corner, public at all times. Register: visitable ja, visible ja, owner gemeente.
transport: Nispen is about 6 km south of Roosendaal station (about 20 minutes by bike or car); a bus connection was not confirmed, check 9292 for the Nispen stop. 650 m from the cemetery beech (roo_012).
story:
Somewhere under this lime's roots lies a bottle with a letter in it. In May 1909 Nispen's Oranje-Comité planted the tree to mark the birth of Princess Juliana on 30 April, and a charter signed by mayor Coenen and the committee members was sealed in the bottle and buried at its foot. The village schoolchildren took part. The two sources disagree by a day on the planting, the 24th or the 25th of May, so May 1909 is as close as anyone can honestly put it.

The princess became queen in 1948. The tree stayed on its grass triangle where Dorpsstraat meets De Lind, and the village kept coming back to it. In 1993 the local history society, Heemkundekring de Heerlijckheijd Nispen, formally adopted the Julianalinde, and its sign was unveiled by Catharina Verhoeven, who had been one of the children at the planting 84 years earlier. For the hundredth year, in 2009, the society held an exhibition at the tree and the Oranje-Comité gave it an orange nest box.

Today it is 2.82 metres round and 18 metres tall, a common lime by the national register's identification. The register last checked it in April 2024 and found it in reasonable condition, with one complaint: the paving has closed in around it, and the inspector advised giving it a better place to grow.

It is free to visit at any hour, 650 metres from the copper beech at the cemetery gate.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the lone lime on the grass triangle where Dorpsstraat meets De Lind, its trunk 2.82 metres round. It stands in the middle of Nispen, 650 metres from the copper beech at the cemetery.

best_time.label: late June into July, when the cream flowers open and the corner hums with bees

name: The Oak of Nispen
age_estimate: roughly 100 years, from a registered planting decade

location.address: Nispen, Essenseweg 35, roadside at the edge of a maize field

access: Free. Stands in the road verge beside the public Essenseweg at the edge of a field, owner gemeente. Register: visitable ja, visible ja, openbaar ja. Open at all times; view from the road.
transport: Nispen is about 6 km south of Roosendaal station (about 20 minutes by bike or car); a bus connection was not confirmed, check 9292 for the Nispen stop. About 320 m from the cemetery copper beech (roo_012).
story:
This oak stands in three places at once: partly in the field, partly in the road verge and partly under the paving of Essenseweg. The national tree register records all three, and at its last visit, in March 2024, the inspector noted that the road did not seem to bother the base of the trunk.

The Bomenstichting's Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen bands its planting to the 1920s, which makes it roughly 96 to 106 years old. It is 3.05 metres round at chest height and 18 metres tall, and it stands on its own at the edge of the farmland.

The register's file puts it in a larger landscape. Nispen, it says, is the oldest settlement for a long way around, and land consolidation, the Dutch ruilverkaveling, redrew the fields here drastically. The file does not say when, or what this tree saw of it. What it does record is a rough patch in August 2003: storm damage and dead wood in the crown, with advice to cut back the suckers and check the base of the trunk for damage. In 2024 the inspector found it in good condition, and the file describes a healthy tree with a fine crown.

That register is the only source we have for this oak, so nobody has written down who planted it or why. If you know, tell us.

It is free to see from the road at any hour, about 320 metres from the copper beech at Nispen's parish cemetery.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the lone oak at the edge of the field on Essenseweg, its trunk 3.05 metres round and partly in the road paving. It stands about 320 metres from the copper beech at the parish cemetery.

name: The Beatrixlinde of Nispen

location.address: Nispen, corner of Bergsebaan and Klokbergsestraat

verified_sources: https://www.heemkundenispen.nl/oranjebomen_beatrixlinde.htm (Heemkundekring de Heerlijckheijd Nispen: Beatrixlinde, memorial tree planted 1 February 1938, adopted 30 April 1993, stands at the corner of Bergsebaan and Klokbergsestraat)
access: Free. Stands on the open gravel verge at a public village street corner (Bergsebaan/Klokbergsestraat), owner gemeente. Register: visitable ja, visible ja, openbaar ja. Open at all times.
transport: Nispen is about 6 km south of Roosendaal station (about 20 minutes by bike or car); a bus connection was not confirmed, check 9292 for the Nispen stop. About 670 m from the cemetery copper beech (roo_012) and 560 m from the Julianalinde (roo_013).
story:
Nispen planted this lime the day after Princess Beatrix was born. She arrived on 31 January 1938, and on 1 February, according to the village's local history society, Nispen went to mass, walked in procession through the streets and put a memorial tree in the ground. Then came a football match, folk games and, after dark, a torchlight procession.

The national tree register agrees on the year, listing it as a Beatrix tree from 1938, and identifies it as an American lime of the cultivar 'Nova', a different species from the common lime Nispen planted for Juliana in 1909. Today it is 2.83 metres round at chest height and 19 metres tall, standing alone on open gravel at the corner of Bergsebaan and Klokbergsestraat. It carries an old frost crack on its south side. The register last checked it in September 2023 and kept it on the list as monumental.

The baby became queen in 1980. On 30 April 1993, Queen's Day, the Heemkundekring de Heerlijckheijd Nispen adopted the tree, and by its own account has decorated it with a few plants every Queen's Day since.

Not every account agrees on which royal tree stands where. A regional history article puts a Juliana tree at this same corner and calls the date of the Beatrix planting unknown. The register and the history society both place the Beatrix lime here, and the question has not been settled.

It is free to visit at any hour, 560 metres from the Julianalinde.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the lone lime on the open gravel at the corner of Bergsebaan and Klokbergsestraat, 2.83 metres round with an old frost crack on its south side. It stands 560 metres from the Julianalinde.

name: The Lebanon Cedar of Villa Van Gilse
age_estimate: roughly 120 years, from a registered planting decade

location.address: Roosendaal, Burgerhoutsestraat 12 (Villa Van Gilse garden, front of the villa)

access: Free. The villa garden is, in the Rijksmonument description, 'thans toegankelijk als park'; LRMB records visitable ja, public ja, owner the municipality. The villa itself is a music school, so stay in the garden. No hours published.
transport: Roosendaal station is about 1.3 km north-west, roughly a 15 minute walk via Stationsstraat and Burgerhoutsestraat.
story:
The national monument listing for Villa Van Gilse names the oaks, a chestnut and a red beech from the years the house was built. It does not mention the cedar on the front lawn.

The tree register does. The Bomenstichting's Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen records a Cedar of Lebanon here, 3.03 metres round at chest height and 23 metres tall, and bands its planting to the decade 1900 to 1910, which makes it roughly 116 to 126 years old. That band is the only basis for its age. We have found no planting record, so whether it belonged to the villa's first garden or arrived a few years later is something nobody has written down. If you know, tell us.

The house behind it was built in 1900 for the factory owner J. van Gilse, to a design by the architect M. Vergouwen, and it is a Rijksmonument today. Since 1975 it has been a music school, and the garden around it is open as a park.

The register last recorded the cedar in August 2023, and an aerial photograph from spring 2026 still shows its crown in place: the only conifer on the front lawn, blue-green while everything around it stood bare.

The same garden holds two other registered trees, a plane and a catalpa, each with its own page here. The building belongs to the music students, so see the cedar from the garden.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the only conifer on the front lawn of Villa Van Gilse, blue-green and evergreen when the trees around it are bare. It is the only cedar the register lists in this garden.
verify_notes: LRMB 1689666 'Libanonceder', planting band 1900-1910 (so about 116 to 126 years; the band is the only age basis, no planting record), girth 303 cm, height 23 m, last observed 2023-08, register photo 2023 (not licensed, not used). Alive: 2023 register observation with photo, and the spring 2026 PDOK frame shows a single blue-green evergreen crown at the register point (the only conifer on the front lawn), so the pin is the crown centre from that frame (register coordinate 51.530519, 4.462506, about 4 m off). Same garden holds already-live roo_004 (catalpa) and roo_009 (plane). Villa Van Gilse is Rijksmonument 517259: factory-owner's villa built 1900 for J. van Gilse, architect M. Vergouwen, music school since 1975; the monument text lists trees from the building period (oaks, a chestnut, a red beech) but does not name the cedar, so do not tie the cedar to the 1900 build. Recognise: the only cedar in the register for this garden; evergreen against bare neighbours. Two sources: LRMB plus RCE monument register (garden access) plus PDOK aerial.

name: The Himalayan Cedar of the Paterstuin
age_estimate: roughly 120 years, from a registered planting decade

location.address: Roosendaal, Kade 23, Paterstuin behind the Onze Lieve Vrouwekerk

access: Free. Garden of the Onze Lieve Vrouwekerk (Kade 21-23), opened to the public as a park on 2015-07-16, open in daylight, gate closes at dusk (2015 municipal report); the gemeente tourism site inroosendaal.nl lists it as a place to visit. Walk right of the church and monastery to the back. Garden stays parish property; the 2015 agreement on opening ran to 2025 and renewal is not confirmed, hence flagged.
transport: Roosendaal station is about 0.5 km east, a 6 minute walk along Kade.
story:
When the Paterstuin was renovated in 2014 and 2015, a beech, a lime and a weeping ash from the national tree register came down. The Himalayan cedar stayed.

It grows in the garden the Redemptorist fathers laid out behind the Onze Lieve Vrouwekerk after 1868: an ornamental garden between two arms of the Watermolenbeek, with a pond, a bridge, a crucifix and a conservatory. Only on 16 July 2015 did it open to the public as a park.

The Bomenstichting's Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen, which spells it 'Hymalaia ceder', bands the cedar's planting to the decade 1900 to 1910, so it is roughly 116 to 126 years old. That band is the only basis for its age, and nobody has recorded who planted it. It is 2.75 metres round at chest height and 18 metres tall, and the register last recorded it in March 2023.

Two honest warnings. Several evergreens stand around the pond, and an aerial photograph cannot tell them apart, so our pin is the register's point rather than a fix at the trunk: look for the cedar, not the pin. And the garden still belongs to the parish. It opens in daylight and the gate closes at dusk, under a 2015 agreement that ran to 2025; we have not confirmed it was renewed. If you find the gate locked in daytime, or the cedar gone, tell us.

A registered horse chestnut stands at the west end of the same garden.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the cedar among the evergreens around the pond, 2.75 metres round and 18 metres tall; it is the only cedar the tree register lists in the Paterstuin. Walk to the right of the church to reach the garden.
verify_notes: LRMB 1680955 'Hymalaia ceder' (Cedrus deodara), band 1900-1910, girth 275 cm, height 18 m, status 3, last observed 2023-03, register photos 2017 and 2023 (not licensed). Alive: 2023 observation; spring 2026 PDOK frame shows several evergreen crowns around the pond, so the individual crown cannot be separated from the aerial and the pin stays the register point, approximate inside a garden about 100 m by 60 m. Small named site: Paterstuin. What tells it apart there: the register lists only one Cedrus in the garden (the other registered trees are chestnut, silver maple, oak, sycamore, lime, ash). Garden: ornamental garden laid out by the Redemptorist fathers after 1868 between two arms of the Watermolenbeek, with pond, bridge, crucifix and conservatory (inroosendaal.nl). Garden was renovated 2014/2015; the register notes several neighbouring trees (beech 1680951, lime 1680950, weeping ash 1690561) were felled then, so the cedar survived that. Shares the site with roo_018 (horse chestnut).

name: The Horse Chestnut of the Paterstuin
age_estimate: roughly 120 years, from a registered planting decade

location.address: Roosendaal, Kade 23, Paterstuin behind the Onze Lieve Vrouwekerk

access: Free. Same garden and conditions as roo_017: open in daylight since 2015, gate closes at dusk, parish property, opening agreement ran to 2025 and renewal is not confirmed.
transport: Roosendaal station is about 0.5 km east, a 6 minute walk along Kade.
story:
Of the horse chestnuts in the row at the west end of the Paterstuin, only one still grows the way a horse chestnut wants to. The national tree register counts three trees, one in natural form and two pruned into candelabras, and records the rest of the row as dead.

The Bomenstichting's Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen bands the row's planting to the decade 1900 to 1910, so it is roughly 116 to 126 years old. It gives one girth for the whole entry, 3.49 metres round at chest height, and a height of 16 metres, without saying which trunk it measured. Read it as the row's figure, not a promise about any one tree.

By that girth, nothing on the register is now larger in this garden. An oak and a sycamore nearby were taken off the monumental list in the latest update for their modest size and condition, and a beech, a lime and a weeping ash were felled when the garden was renovated in 2014 and 2015.

The Redemptorist fathers laid the garden out after 1868, and it opened as a public park on 16 July 2015. It is still parish ground, open in daylight with the gate closing at dusk, under an agreement that ran to 2025 and that we have not confirmed was renewed. Our pin is the register's point, so look for the row rather than the pin, and tell us if you find the gate shut.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the chestnut row at the west end of the Paterstuin: one tree with a full natural crown beside two pruned into candelabras. The garden lies behind the Onze Lieve Vrouwekerk, to the right of the church.
verify_notes: LRMB 1680952, band 1900-1910, girth 349 cm, height 16 m, last observed 2023-03, register photos 2017 and 2023 (not licensed). Register counts 3 in a row (aantal_bomen 3) and says: one tree of the row is still in natural form, two are candelabra-pruned and the rest dead; girth is the register's single figure for the entry, taken to be the natural-form tree but the register does not say so, so treat 349 cm as the entry's figure. Neighbours in the same garden were re-evaluated to non-monumental in the latest update (oak 1680953, sycamore 1680954) for modest size and condition, so this chestnut is the largest standing in the garden by the register. Pin is the register point (51.53323, 4.45015), approximate; small named site Paterstuin. What tells it apart: the chestnut row at the west end of the garden, one in natural crown, two pollarded (sources only). Do not claim it is the only chestnut.

name: The Sycamore at the Border
age_estimate: roughly 130 years, from a registered planting decade

location.address: Nispen, Grensstraat 2, just before the Belgian border

access: Visible from the public road Grensstraat. Register: owner municipality, visitable ja, public ja, setting listed as pasture (weiland), so view it from the road edge; no hours.
transport: No rail. About 1.9 km south of the centre of Nispen (De Lind), roughly a 25 minute walk; no bus stop was checked.
story:
Around 2001 or 2002, workers laid a deep sewer under the road beside this sycamore and cut away the roots that ran beneath it. When the inspectors came back in 2003, the tree showed no loss of condition at all.

The national tree register gives it a name that doubles as directions: 'Esdoorn net voor de grens', the maple just before the border. It stands at Grensstraat 2, south of Nispen, with Belgium a short way further down the road.

The Bomenstichting's Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen bands its planting to the decade 1890 to 1900, which makes it roughly 126 to 136 years old. It is 2.96 metres round at chest height and 18 metres tall. The register last recorded it in April 2023, and an aerial photograph from spring 2026 still shows its crown at the edge of the grass, with no other tree within about 30 metres.

That register is the only source we have for this sycamore. Nobody has written down who planted it, or why a sycamore went in here on the border road. If you know, tell us.

The ground it stands on is listed as pasture, so look from the road edge rather than walking in. There is no train out here: it is about 1.9 kilometres south of the village centre at De Lind, roughly a 25 minute walk, and 1.4 kilometres beyond the oak of Nispen.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the lone tree at the edge of the grass beside Grensstraat, no other tree within about 30 metres, its trunk 2.96 metres round. It stands at number 2, just before the Belgian border.
verify_notes: LRMB 1690592 'Esdoorn net voor de grens' (register name), band 1890-1900, girth 296 cm, height 18 m, status 3, last observed 2023-04, register photo 2023 (not licensed). Register note: in 2001/2002 a deep sewer was laid and roots under the road removed, no condition loss visible at the 2003 inspection; so the roots lost on the road side are a fact the writer may use. Alive: 2023 observation with photo; spring 2026 PDOK frame shows one bare crown on the register point at the verge of a lawn beside the road, no other tree within about 30 m, so pin held as confirmed, but the crown sits in shadow in a leafless frame, so this is a modest confirmation. Register only, flagged (no second source; transport stop not checked). Nearest published trees: roo_014 oak of Nispen about 1.4 km north.
